The Big Question HL

🤔 How can a website find a username in a database of millions…

in a fraction of a second?

❌ Common misconception: "It's just faster computers."

Hardware helps, but data structure choices often matter more.

✅ Reality: the right abstract data type can reduce work from O(n) to O(1) or O(log n).

That's the difference between "scan everything" and "jump straight to it".

HL What is an ADT?

Why describe "what it does" separately from "how it's built"?

An ADT is defined by its interface (operations).

You can change the implementation without changing how users interact with it.

This is abstraction.

Example: Set ADT

# Interface (what it does)
set.add(item)
set.remove(item)
set.contains(item)

# Implementation could be:
# - Hash table (fast)
# - Balanced tree (ordered)

HL Linked Lists

What if you need a structure that can grow and shrink efficiently?

A linked list is made of nodes.

Each node stores data + a pointer to the next node.

The head points to the first node.

Visual

head → [A|→] → [B|→] → [C|→] → None

HL Linked List in Python

class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

class LinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None
    
    def insert_at_head(self, data):
        new_node = Node(data)
        new_node.next = self.head  # Point to old head
        self.head = new_node       # Update head

Key: Insertion at head is O(1) — no traversal needed!

HL Types of Linked Lists

Singly Linked

Each node points to next only.

A → B → C → None

Doubly Linked

Each node has next and prev pointers.

None ← A ⇄ B ⇄ C → None

Press Down for Circular

Circular Linked List

Tail points back to head → continuous traversal.

A → B → C → (back to A)

Use case: Round-robin scheduling, circular buffers.

HL Linked List Complexity

Operation Time Why?
Insert at head O(1) Just update head pointer
Insert at tail O(n) Must traverse to find tail
Search O(n) Must traverse node-by-node
Delete (with pointer) O(1) Just redirect pointers

Trade-off: No random access like arrays (arr[5]), but efficient insertion/deletion.

HL Binary Search Trees (BSTs)

How can a tree make searching faster than O(n)?

A BST organises data so:

Left subtree < node < Right subtree

Each comparison eliminates half the tree!

Example BST

      8
     / \
    3   10
   / \    \
  1   6   14

HL BST Search in Python

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def search_bst(root, target):
    if root is None:
        return False
    if target == root.value:
        return True
    elif target < root.value:
        return search_bst(root.left, target)
    else:
        return search_bst(root.right, target)

Complexity: O(log n) average, O(n) worst-case (if unbalanced).

HL Hash Tables

How can we look up values in O(1) average time?

A hash table converts keys to array indices.

Key → hash function → index → value

# Python dict is a hash table
phonebook = {}
phonebook["Alice"] = "555-1234"
phonebook["Bob"] = "555-5678"

# O(1) average lookup
print(phonebook["Alice"])

HL Collisions & Resolution

What if two keys hash to the same index?

Chaining

Each slot holds a linked list.

Multiple items at same index.

Open Addressing

Probe for next empty slot.

Linear probing: check slot+1, +2, ...

Load factor = items ÷ table size. When high, rehash to restore O(1).

HL Sets in Python

What makes a set different from a list?

Sets contain unique elements only.

No duplicates, no ordering.

A = {1, 2, 3}
B = {3, 4}

print(A | B)  # Union: {1, 2, 3, 4}
print(A & B)  # Intersection: {3}
print(A - B)  # Difference: {1, 2}
print(3 in A) # Membership: True

🧠 Quick Check HL

1. What is the average time complexity of hash table lookup?

O(1) — constant time

2. When would a BST degrade to O(n) search?

When the tree is unbalanced (e.g., all nodes to one side)

Misconception Check

A. Linked lists allow O(1) random access like arrays.

B. Hash table operations are always O(1).

C. A balanced BST provides O(log n) search.

D. Sets automatically remove duplicate elements.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Linked lists require O(n) traversal — no direct indexing.

B: False. Collisions can degrade to O(n); average is O(1).

C: True. Balanced trees halve search space each step.

D: True. Sets enforce uniqueness by definition.

Key Takeaways HL

  • ADT = interface (what) vs implementation (how).
  • Linked list: O(1) insert at head, O(n) search — dynamic size.
  • BST: O(log n) operations when balanced.
  • Hash table: O(1) average — handle collisions with chaining/probing.
  • Set: unique elements, union/intersection/difference operations.

Exam tip: Always justify data structure choices with operation needs + complexity.
